Testimony of the Maine Association of Independent Schools
In Support of
LD 974, Resolve, to Increase the High School Graduation Rate by Creating the Maine Promise Initiative
Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
March 26, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Members of the Education Committee,
My name is Daniel Walker with Preti Flaherty, and I testify on behalf of the Maine Association of Independent Schools (MAIS) in support of LD 974, Resolve, to Increase the High School Graduation Rate by Creating the Maine Promise Initiative.
MAIS 23 members are a diverse group of educational institutions, including Maine's earliest secondary school (Berwick Academy) dating to the 18th century with charters signed by Governor John Hancock, as well as much newer schools, schools with varied missions, schools which serve primarily public-tuition students, and one sectarian school. MAIS schools educate about 9000 students in pre-K through Grade 12, with 4600 publicly funded and 4400 privately funded. What all MAIS schools have in common is their accreditation by the New England Association of Schools and Colleges.
I first want to thank Rep. Brennan for bringing forward this resolve and the important issue of increasing high school graduation rates. Rep. Brennan importantly focuses on not only generally increasing the rate to at least 95% across the state but also focusing on identified populations of students that are historically below the current graduation rates, including unhoused students, Native American students, students in the child welfare system, and students in the juvenile justice system.
The Resolve directs the Department of Education to convene a working group of interested stakeholders to develop a strategic plan to implement the initiative and achieve its goals. MAIS schools would like to be part of the diverse array of stakeholders tasked with accomplishing this important work.
In many communities in Maine, the MAIS schools are developing and implementing strategies to retain a vast range of students, allowing them to thrive straight through until graduation. Many MAIS schools bring a different perspective to tackling the same challenges of resources, community partnerships, coordination with local and state programs, and personnel.
Again, thank you for bringing this important legislation forward, and MAIS would like to be part of the solution.

RESOLVE, TO INCREASE THE HIGH SCHOOL GRADUATION RATE BY CREATING THE MAINE PROMISE INITIATIVE
March 26, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee, I am Eileen King, the executive director for the Maine School Superintendents Association, testifying on behalf of the MSSA legislative committee neither for nor against L.D. 974.
L.D. 974 seeks to establish the Maine Promise Initiative with the goal of increasing high school graduation rates to at least 95% by 2030, including specific targets for identified student populations who face systemic challenges. The resolve outlines the creation of a strategic plan by the Department of Education and a one-time appropriation of $100,000 to support the initiative's development.
The intent behind this proposal--to improve educational outcomes and ensure more students complete their secondary education--is commendable. A high school diploma is a critical milestone that can open pathways to post-secondary education, career opportunities, and longterm economic stability. Targeting support for student populations who historically experience lower graduation rates is also an important step in addressing educational equity, and focusing on those populations can help our state to target specific strategies and instructional approaches to help these students succeed.
However, there are considerations that warrant further discussion. The initiative's success will likely depend on a comprehensive and sustainable implementation plan beyond the initial appropriation. Ensuring that school districts have the necessary resources, personnel, and community partnerships to support students at risk of not graduating will be critical. Additionally, coordination with existing state and local programs aimed at dropout prevention, alternative education pathways, and student support services should be a key component of the initiative. We believe that adult education needs to be a key part of any conversations, as well. More and more students are turning to adult education to receive a high school degree, and the incorporation and recognition of these efforts must be recognized.

The working group tasked with developing the strategic plan should include a diverse range of stakeholders, including school administrators, educators, students, and community organizations, to ensure the initiative is both practical and responsive to the needs of Maine's students. Furthermore, ongoing assessment and transparent reporting will be essential in determining the effectiveness of the initiative and whether adjustments are needed to meet its ambitious goals.
L.D. 974 presents a well-intended effort to increase high school graduation rates in Maine. While its success will depend on strong planning, adequate resources, and stakeholder collaboration, the resolve provides a foundation for further discussion on how best to support students on their path to graduation.

Leading for equity, excellence and opportunity for all Maine Students

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Distinguished Members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee:
LD 974, Resolve, to Increase the High School Graduation Rate by Creating the Maine Promise Initiative, would direct the Department of Education (DOE) to create the Maine Promise Initiative, with the goal to raise high school graduation rates in Maine above 95% by the year 2030. To craft this initiative, the DOE would be directed establish a working group to develop the strategic plan and goals of this initiative, with a report due back to the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee by December 3, 2025.
The tables on the following pages show Maine's most recent high school graduation rate, broken down by 4-year, 5-year, and 6-year graduation cohorts.
There are numerous known barriers to graduation that our students face, including poverty, housing instability, involvement in the foster care system, and being a multilingual learner. When examining graduation rates through each of these lenses, we see a pattern emerge.
For students who are not economically disadvantaged, the graduation rates are around 95% already. For those who are economically disadvantaged, their graduation rate is approximately 15 points lower than their non-economically disadvantaged peers as indicated in Table 2. It is important to note that economically disadvantaged youth make up at least 45% of each cohort.
Table 3 demonstrates how experiencing homelessness has a dramatically negative impact on graduation rates. For each cohort, students experiencing homelessness have graduation rates of 25-30 points lower than their peers. Homeless youth make up between 3.5 and 5.5% of each cohort.
Experience in the foster care system also has a dramatically negative impact on graduation rates. For each cohort, foster youth have graduation rates approximately 25 points lower than their peers. Foster youth make up less than 1% of each cohort, as seen in Table 4.

Students who are designated as multilingual learners are learning English while engaging in all aspects of their school experience. These students' experience is shown on Table 5. This is another significant barrier for graduation rates, which are 12-20 points lower than their peers. Multilingual learners make up between 3 and 4.5% of each cohort.
All of the data shared above can be found on the Maine DOE website: https://www.maine.gov/doe/data-warehouse/reporting/graduation.
At the Maine Department of Education, promoting high graduation rates is an ongoing priority. There are numerous initiatives and programmatic offerings with the intent to make a positive impact on high school graduation rates. Some of the strategies utilized by the Maine DOE include:
 Attendance and engagement work: The Office of School and Student Supports provides resources and guidance to help schools monitor and reduce chronic absenteeism. The office supports school attendance and intervention teams at Maine school administrative units, assists families in understanding school attendance requirements and exploring learning options, and partners with other agencies to coordinate a community approach to making school attendance a priority in Maine.
 Building Assets, Reducing Risks (BARR System): BARR is a system where schools adopt BARR's eight interconnected strategies, including: 1. focus on the whole student; 2. provide professional development for teachers, counselors, and administrators; 3. use BARR's curriculum to foster a climate for learning and relationship building; 4. create cohorts to cultivate connections; 5. hold regular meetings of the cohort teacher teams to discuss each student; 6. conduct "Community Connect" meetings that engage the community; 7. engage families, and 8. engage administrators. BARR schools report higher student and family engagement, which directly impacts graduation rates.
 Extended learning opportunities: The Office of Workforce Development and Innovative Pathways provides support for districts to utilize extended learning opportunities, which are credit-bearing experiences in which students explore careers of interest. Extended Learning Opportunities, along with other nontraditional approaches, help bolster student engagement in their learning and can lead to higher graduation rates.
 Supporting educators: The Office of School and Student Supports provides a train-thetrainer model that has anecdotally reduced teacher burnout and supported classroom management with the increased student behaviors seen since COVID. This model is a Tier-4 evidence-based approach The Regulated Classroom, founded and written by former New Hampshire school counselor Emily Reed Daniels. By educating school personnel on the science of regulation and trauma, Maine educators are equipping themselves with tools and strategies.
 Supporting families: The Office of School and Student Supports secured a partnership with Mid-Atlantic Equity (MAEC) in 2022 to create a Statewide Family Engagement Center. This Center for Engaging Families Across Maine (also known as CEFAM) has provided 5,000 licenses to families across Maine for a text-based curricula on child development and learning milestones; has awarded subgrants to CAP agencies and Maine

Good morning, Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonen Murphy and fellow distinguished
members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs. My name is
Michael Brennan, and I represent House District 115, which includes a portion of Portland.
Today, I am here to introduce LD 974, Resolve, to Increase the High School Graduation Rate
by Creating the Maine Promise Initiative.
This measure would direct the Department of Education (DOE) to create the Maine Promise
Initiative,
which would work to achieve a 95% high school graduation rate by 2030 within a 4 or 6-year
time period.

Further, this program will include increasing the graduation rates for identified populations that are currently below the 2025 graduation rates of Maine's general population of secondary school
students. The DOE will be directed to report out the progress of their efforts to this committee.
According to the Maine Education Policy Research Institute's (MEPRI) March 2025 Report on Analysis of Maine's High School Graduation Rates, Maine's statewide high school graduation
rate was 86% in spring 2022 which is consistent with the national average of 87%. While this is good news, we are seeing data that suggests a significant number of certain populations are

from high school from 2011 to 2022. As stated in the report, most of the student subgroups
examined have considerably lower graduation rates than the total student population.
